cim: STALLARD: Artificial intelligence can't replace the real kind
cim_eredeti: STALLARD: Artificial intelligence can't replace the real kind
szoveg_eredeti:
The ongoing discussions regarding artificial intelligence are real, even if some of the stuff AI is producing is not.

A while back, I learned how to use a specific form of AI to restore old photos. Some of those I tried were very old family photos, including the only pic I have of my mother and grandmother together. The original was an old black-and-white image, one of those shot on film and developed at the nearby pharmacy or whomever processed film in those days.

The old pic was pretty hazy and faded, with white spots because of its age and time in a photo album.

I thought I’d give it a shot. Ran it through the AI thingy, and the result took my breath.

Crystal clear, man. The faces in the restored pic were just as I remembered them, down to the smallest detail.

I tried another one — a pic of my brothers and me with our dad, a photo not even as old as the one of my mom and grandmother. Heck, this one was even in color, albeit a little hazy.

I don’t know who the new guys in the restored pic are, but they ain’t us. Not even close.

I even tried clearing up a sports photo I shot recently. I loved the action in it, but it was a tiny bit out of focus.

Now, my journalism background wasn’t gonna let me submit an AI-restored photo for publication, but I wanted the kid to have it anyway.

Until AI finished with it. The kid suddenly had a third ear, and the lettering on his jersey looked like some kind of hieroglyphics.

So you’re telling me maybe artificial intelligence isn’t quite as intelligent as advertised?

I’m also seeing more and more examples of relying on AI for written work. I once read an AI-generated recap of a sporting event. There were numerous errors, not the least of which were the final score (wrong) and the winning team (also wrong).

If I hadn’t been tracking the game myself, I wouldn’t have known any better. I’d have just gone with whatever the AI told me.

Therein lies my biggest issue with the use of artificial intelligence: Accuracy. Sometimes it’s spot-on, such as the pic of my mother and grandmother. Other times, it’s adding a third ear, or giving us wrong information altogether. Yay, wrong team.

One might think that would be enough reason to eschew AI altogether, but one would be wrong.

AI ain’t going anywhere, y’all. It’s here to stay.

Admittedly, it has its value. Not long ago, I was able to listen in on a panel consisting of business and state leaders, and they fielded questions on the future of artificial intelligence. Some examples related how technicians in certain fields can use prompts to get quick answers from artificial intelligence, saving countless hours of analysis. The technician then can get straight to work on a problem rather than spending all that time troubleshooting.

For the business, it means an increase in productivity and profits. Who wouldn’t want such a scenario?

But even the business owners acknowledged that blind trust in AI isn’t realistic. There still has to be a human element involved to ensure the information is both accurate and useful.

Then came the discussion on the “ethical” use of artificial intelligence, and I’m learning certain necessary boundaries.

Using AI as a tool for one’s own work can be a good thing. A student can use it to check spelling and grammar on a written assignment, for example. Or a photographer can use certain forms of AI to sharpen an image. Those are examples of a person creating his or her own work and simply using the best available tools for improvement.

However — and here’s where it’s getting weird — using AI to create work is not only risky, but it’s unethical. I mean, I could probably type in a prompt asking AI to create an image or video for me, and it’s gonna do it. I probably could have entered a prompt asking AI to write this whole column for me, and it would have done it.

All I’d have to do afterward is slap my name on it and call it mine.

Not only would I have been wrong in doing so, but I wouldn’t have been able to guarantee the provided information was factual.

Want proof? Just look at some of the stuff currently flooding social media. Some are done for obvious fun, but still others are created with the sole intention of deceiving. I’ve seen it named “AI Slop” by people who recognize it for what it is.

Not everyone has those recognition factors, unfortunately. Too many think because they can see or read it, it’s gotta be legit. I admit to falling for a fake image at first, only to realize I was being duped after closer inspection.

I understand the fears of our entire future society getting overrun by AI agents. Taking all our jobs. Doing all our thinking and decision making for us.

But from what I’m seeing and learning so far, AI’s not yet ready for the full-on takeover.

We still need plenty of real intelligence to handle all the artificial stuff.

Gary Stallard is a regular contributor to the Opinion page of The Lufkin Daily News. His email address is garylstallard@gmail.com.
